prohibited_recommendations: Do not start a cholinesterase inhibitor (donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine): no benefit in FTD, NICE NG97 advises against it, and it may worsen behaviour.
Do not start memantine: a randomised trial showed no benefit in FTD and NICE NG97 advises against it.
Avoid antipsychotics as first-line behavioral therapy given increased cerebrovascular and mortality risk in dementia; reserve for refractory dangerous agitation with specialist oversight.
Avoid benzodiazepines for behavioral control: risk of paradoxical disinhibition and falls.
required_recommendations: Apply the Rascovsky 2011 criteria: state which features are present, the functional decline, and the level of certainty (possible or probable).

Explain why alcohol-related brain damage does not account for the progressive syndrome, and manage the all-day drinking as part of the behavioural change (limit access, involve his wife, support abstinence).
Address safety and capacity: driving, finances (large unilateral financial decisions) and lasting power of attorney while he can still take part.
Arrange caregiver education and support, and a plan for behavioural symptoms that avoids cholinesterase inhibitors and memantine.
Offer genetic counselling before any genetic test, and discuss what a result would mean for relatives, given his brother's FTD and his father's personality change in his 60s.
Review for emerging motor neuron disease (fasciculations, wasting, dysarthria, dysphagia) at follow-up, as familial bvFTD can evolve into FTD-ALS.

avoided_actions.rationale: EEG is non-specific in FTD; not part of the standard dementia workup unless seizures or rapidly progressive course suggest CJD or autoimmune encephalitis.
ECG has no role in the cognitive workup of suspected FTD; reserved for syncope, palpitations, or pre-procedure clearance.
Echocardiography is unrelated to a neurodegenerative cognitive syndrome and adds cost without diagnostic value.
Ambulatory cardiac monitoring is unrelated to FTD and not indicated absent syncope or palpitations.
Non-contrast head CT lacks the resolution and lobar specificity needed to characterise frontotemporal atrophy; MRI is the standard structural study.
MR spectroscopy has no established role in the routine FTD diagnostic pathway.
Perfusion MRI is not part of the FTD work-up; FDG-PET, or perfusion SPECT where it is unavailable, is the functional study used when needed.
Carotid duplex is a vascular study with no diagnostic role in primary neurodegenerative dementia.
DaTscan evaluates presynaptic dopaminergic terminals; he has no parkinsonism and it would not change the diagnosis.

key_clinical_evidence: Three Rascovsky features on his wife's account (disinhibition, compulsive checking and rules, hyperorality including the drinking), with loss of his job, meet possible bvFTD with significant functional decline.
Severe bilateral frontal and anterior temporal atrophy with a knife-blade pattern, normal hippocampi and preserved posterior cortex on MRI give the imaging support for probable bvFTD.
Neuropsychology shows severe executive and social-cognition deficits with normal recognition memory and visuospatial function.
The frontal and anterior temporal pattern with relative posterior sparing makes Alzheimer disease less likely; an amyloid or CSF AD biomarker study is optional if doubt remains.
An affected sibling strengthens the indication to offer genetic counselling and optional testing but does not make testing mandatory for the clinical diagnosis.

Familial behavioural variant FTD genetic.summary: Rascovsky and colleagues (2011) define possible behavioural variant FTD by three of six behavioural and cognitive features, probable bvFTD by added functional decline and frontal or anterior temporal involvement on structural or functional imaging, and definite bvFTD by histopathology or a pathogenic mutation. C9orf72 expansions and GRN and MAPT variants cause most familial FTD; counselling precedes any genetic test and any predictive testing of relatives. Treatment is supportive: SSRIs or trazodone for behaviour, caregiver support and safety planning; cholinesterase inhibitors and memantine are not recommended.

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. B. is a 57-year-old right-handed White male engineer referred by his wife for progressive personality and behavioral changes over 18 months. He was fired from his engineering job one year ago after persistent conflicts with management and HR complaints from female coworkers about inappropriate remarks. His wife describes a dramatic change: he has become impulsive, making large unilateral financial decisions, and confrontational, arguing loudly with neighbors over minor issues. He exhibits perseverative behaviors including repeatedly checking door locks (up to 50 times nightly), demanding the TV volume stay at exactly 24. He overeats compulsively, consuming entire boxes of cereal in one sitting. He consumes alcohol throughout the day, denying this is abnormal. He shows no remorse or insight. Family history is highly significant: his brother, age 53, was recently diagnosed with FTD at another institution, and their father had notable personality changes in his 60s but died before evaluation.
